warmup.q: Your ledger service and your fraud-check service consume the payments topic as two consumer groups. The ledger group has read and committed everything. Fraud check is 3,000 records behind. What happens to the records the ledger group has already read?
options: Kafka deletes them as soon as the ledger group commits its offset
They stay until the topic's retention removes them, whoever has read them
Kafka keeps them until the fraud-check group has read them too, then deletes them
Kafka moves them to a backlog that only the fraud-check group can see
warmup.why: Reading never deletes anything in Kafka. Each group keeps one number per partition: the offset of the next record it will read. Records leave only when retention removes old segment files (lesson 3 of this track), on a time or size limit that ignores readers. The first and third options describe the broker queue of lesson 1, which deletes a message once it is acknowledged; that is the habit to unlearn here.

sections.h: Why a log: keep every event, and let each reader keep one number
sections.html:
Lesson 1 sent the payment events through a broker queue, and the queue did its job. No payment was lost while the fraud check was down for a deploy, and the payment service no longer called anyone directly. Lesson 1 also showed what a queue gives up. It keeps a state for every message (ready, unacked, delivered to whom) and deletes the message once a consumer has acked it. To feed four services you need four queues, one copy of every event in each. A fifth team that wants the payments starts with nothing, because last week's events are gone. When a bug in the fee calculation means yesterday's payments must be processed again, the queue can't give them back. And the instances of one service, competing for one queue, booked an account's events out of order.

A log makes the opposite choice: keep the events, and let each reader track its own place. The payment service appends each event to the end of a file that only grows. Every event gets a number, its position in that file: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each reading service remembers one thing, the number of the next event it wants. Reading changes nothing in the file. So four services, or forty, read the same events at their own pace from one copy, a new service can start at event 0, and processing yesterday again means moving one number back.

That growing file is a log: an ordered sequence of records that only grows at the end. Keep this picture for the whole track: one file you only append to, and a bookmark per reader. Every later lesson of this track splits this log up, copies it to other machines or reads it in a cleverer way.

A few names before going on. A record is one event in the log; in Kafka it has a key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers. In Kafka, a broker is the server process that keeps logs on its disk and answers clients over the network. A producer is a client that appends records, and a consumer is a client that reads them. A topic is the name they use, such as payments. Kafka stores each topic as one or more partitions, and each partition is one log. This lesson uses topics with a single partition, so here topic, partition and log mean the same thing. Lesson 3 of this track splits a topic into many partitions.

video.title: The log: appends, offsets and one bookmark per reader

sections.h: The broker numbers every record: offsets
sections.html:
Here is a log after the payment service appended five records. You will build exactly this one in the Try-it below:

offset  key      value
0       acct-17  auth 40.00 EUR
1       acct-42  auth 12.50 EUR
2       acct-17  capture 40.00 EUR
3       acct-99  auth 300.00 EUR
4       acct-42  refund 12.50 EUR

The number on the left is the record's offset: its position in the log, counting from 0. The broker assigns it when the record arrives. The producer never picks it; it learns the number from the broker's reply:

Java
var record = new ProducerRecord<>("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR");
RecordMetadata md = producer.send(record).get();   // waits for the broker's reply
System.out.println(md.offset());                   // the broker chose this number
Kotlin
val record = ProducerRecord("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR")
val md = producer.send(record).get()               // waits for the broker's reply
println(md.offset())                               // the broker chose this number

Three rules make offsets useful. First, an offset never changes: record 2 is the capture for account 17 today, next week and in every replay. Second, Kafka never reuses an offset within a partition. Even after old records are deleted (lesson 3 of this track shows how), the next record gets the next number: if offsets 0 to 799 existed and the oldest 300 were deleted, the next record still gets 800. Third, nothing is inserted or edited. You can't put a record between 1 and 2, and you can't change record 3. To correct something, you append a new record. That's why the capture and the refund above are records of their own: the log is the history of what happened, in the order it happened.

Together these rules make an offset a permanent name for one record. When a consumer says "I have processed everything before offset 4", or an incident ticket says "look at offset 3", everyone means the same record.

One more number. The end offset is the offset the next record will get: 5 in the log above. Kafka's tools call it the log end offset, or LEO. Everything below it exists; nothing at or above it has been written yet.

You have seen this structure before. Oracle writes every change to its redo log before it touches a table, and PostgreSQL does the same with its write-ahead log. Jay Kreps, one of Kafka's creators, built his 2013 essay "The Log" on that idea: if several systems read the same ordered log and apply it the same way, they all end up in the same state. Kafka turns such a log into a service that many systems share.

try.title: Append five payments and read them back
steps: From the labs folder, start the single-node broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait. It is ready in about 5 seconds.

Open a shell in it with docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash and run the commands below. They create a one-partition topic, append five keyed payments and read them back with their offsets.
Predict, then run the consumer command a second time. Which offsets come back?
Keep the broker and the shell open. The next Try-its use them.

code.title: inside the kafka container
code.html: cd /opt/kafka/bin ./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic payments --partitions 1 printf 'acct-17:auth 40.00 EUR\nacct-42:auth 12.50 EUR\nacct-17:capture 40.00 EUR\nacct-99:auth 300.00 EUR\nacct-42:refund 12.50 EUR\n' \ | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments \ --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: ./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments --from-beginning \ --max-messages 5 --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true

try.expect:
Created topic payments.
The consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848) is production-ready! Set group.protocol=consumer to try it out. ...
Offset:0	acct-17	auth 40.00 EUR
Offset:1	acct-42	auth 12.50 EUR
Offset:2	acct-17	capture 40.00 EUR
Offset:3	acct-99	auth 300.00 EUR
Offset:4	acct-42	refund 12.50 EUR
Processed a total of 5 messages

The second run prints the same five lines: the first read removed nothing. The KIP-848 line is a notice the Kafka 4.4 tools print about the new consumer group protocol (lesson 8 of this track). The older --property flag still works in 4.4 but is deprecated; --reader-property and --formatter-property are the new names.

sections.h: A reader's position is one number
sections.html:
Every reader has to remember where it is, so that after a restart it neither skips records nor processes them twice. What is the least it can store?

The queue of lesson 1 stores state per message: delivered to whom, acknowledged or not, returned how often. With a million messages and four consumer services, that's four million entries for the broker to keep. A log needs far less. Its records are in a fixed order and never change, so a reader that has handled everything before offset 50 can describe its whole state with one number: 50. That number is the reader's position, the offset of the next record it will read. Kafka's design doc says it directly: per partition, a consumer's position is a single integer. Reading means asking the broker for records starting at the position, then moving the position past what came back.

A position kept only in memory is lost when the process restarts. So consumers that work together form a consumer group: a named set of consumers that read a topic as one, such as the group ledger. The group saves its position in Kafka itself, in an internal topic called __consumer_offsets. Saving it is a commit, and the saved number is the committed offset. The KafkaConsumer javadoc is clear that it should be the offset of the next record your application will read, not the last one it finished. Get that wrong by one and every restart skips a record or repeats one. Lesson 7 of this track covers commits in depth.

You don't need a group just to read. A consumer can take a partition directly with assign and set its position with seek:

Java
TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0);   // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(List.of(tp));     // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50);            // the next poll starts at offset 50
ConsumerRecords<String, String> batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
Kotlin
val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0)                    // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(listOf(tp))       // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50)             // the next poll starts at offset 50
val batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))

Because a position is only a number, rewinding is cheap. You fixed a bug in the fee calculation and need to recompute yesterday's settlement batch? Seek back and read again. A new reporting service needs history? It starts at the oldest offset Kafka still has. Neither one changes anything for any other reader.

One thing about poll: it returns whatever the broker had ready within the timeout, up to max.poll.records (500 by default). That can be fewer records than you wanted, or none at all, especially on the first call while the client is still connecting. Code that needs "the next 10 records" has to loop until it has them or a deadline passes. You write that loop in the lab.

try.title: Read from offset 50 in Java or Kotlin
steps: Keep the broker from the previous Try-it running. Open ReadFromOffsetDemo.java or its Kotlin twin. It creates the topic payment-events, appends 100 records, then reads 5 of them starting at offset 50.
Run it from the labs folder with the command below.
Predict before you run it a second time: at which offsets will the next 100 records land, and what will the read from offset 50 return? Then run it again.

code.title: ReadFromOffsetDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l02.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata; import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition; import org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TopicExistsException; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.time.Duration; import java.time.LocalTime; import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** Appends 100 payments to a one-partition topic, then reads 5 of them back starting at offset 50. */ public class ReadFromOffsetDemo { static final String TOPIC = "payment-events"; static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; // env/kafka.yml public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. make sure the topic exists: one partition, so one log try (Admin admin = Admin.create(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(TOPIC, 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (!(e.getCause() instanceof TopicExistsException)) throw e; } // 2. append 100 records; the broker answers each one with the offset it got String sentAt = LocalTime.now().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS).toString(); try (var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class))) { List<Future<RecordMetadata>> acks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { acks.add(producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(TOPIC, "acct-" + (i % 7), "payment-" + i + " sent at " + sentAt))); } long first = acks.get(0).get().offset(); long last = acks.get(99).get().offset(); System.out.printf("appended 100 records at offsets %d..%d%n", first, last); } // 3. read 5 records starting at offset 50: no group, just assign and seek TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(TOPIC, 0); try (var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); consumer.seek(tp, 50); System.out.println("reading from offset 50:"); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> got = new ArrayList<>(); while (got.size() < 5) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { if (got.size() < 5) got.add(r); } } for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : got) { System.out.printf(" offset %d key %s value %s%n", r.offset(), r.key(), r.value()); } System.out.printf("end offset of the partition: %d%n", consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp)); } } }

sections.h: Reading does not delete, so every reader gets everything
sections.html:
Since no read removes anything, what does? Only retention: a limit per topic on how old or how large the data may get. By default Kafka keeps a topic's data for 7 days (retention.ms is 604800000 milliseconds) and then deletes the old part, a whole file at a time. Who has read what plays no part. Lesson 3 of this track shows the files and the rules.

Any number of consumer groups can read the same partition, and each group gets every record. Your ledger service and your fraud check are two groups. Each has its own committed offset, and neither can move the other's.

Several things follow from this, and each one comes back later in this track.

A slow consumer does not slow down the producer or the other groups. It just falls behind. This is the log's answer to lesson 1's first question: it buffers on disk, up to retention, instead of pushing back on producers. The distance between the end offset and a group's committed offset is its lag. If the end offset is 1,250 and the fraud check has committed 40, its lag is 1,210 records.

A consumer that crashes starts again from its last committed offset. Whatever it processed after that commit, it processes again. Kafka's default promise is therefore at-least-once delivery: every record is processed at least once, and some may be processed twice. That is why payment consumers need idempotency keys.

Replay is cheap and safe. A new group can read a topic from the oldest offset still kept, and an existing group can move its committed offset back.

Order exists only inside one partition. Two partitions are two separate logs, and nothing orders a record in one against a record in the other. Lesson 3 of this track deals with that.

Kafka 4.2 made share groups production-ready: they hand each record to one member of a group and acknowledge records one by one, like the queue of lesson 1, on top of a topic. Lesson 11 of this track covers them. Every lesson before that uses ordinary consumer groups, which work as described here.

sections.h: Why appending is fast: sequential I/O and the page cache
sections.html:
A busy broker might take 50,000 records a second. Can a disk keep up with that?

It depends on where the writes go. A spinning disk has to move its head to the right track before each write, and a seek takes about 5 to 10 ms, so random writes top out at a few hundred per second. Writing at the end of one file needs almost no seeking: the head stays where it is and the data streams on. Kafka's design doc gives the numbers from its test disks: about 600 MB/s for linear writes against about 100 kB/s for random ones. An NVMe SSD narrows the gap a lot (a random 4 KB read takes about 0.1 ms), but sequential I/O still wins, and it lets the operating system do most of the work.

That work happens in the page cache: spare RAM in which the kernel keeps copies of recently read and written file data. When the broker appends to a log file, the kernel puts the bytes in the page cache and writes them to disk a little later. When a consumer reads near the end of the log, which describes almost every healthy consumer, the data it wants was written seconds ago and is still in RAM. Copying 4 KB from RAM takes well under a microsecond, against about 100 microseconds from an SSD.

Kafka does not keep its own cache of records on the JVM heap; it leans on the page cache. That's why brokers usually run with a heap of a few gigabytes on machines with far more RAM: the rest is page cache.

Two more choices keep the cost down. Records travel in batches: the producer groups records that go to the same partition, and in the common case the broker stores the batch as it arrived and hands it to consumers the same way. And when it can, the broker uses the sendfile system call to send file data from the page cache straight to the network socket, without copying it through the JVM. That zero-copy path is not used when TLS is on, because encryption has to happen in user space.

Finding a record is cheap too. An append is O(1): it goes at the end, however long the log is. A read at an offset finds the right file, looks up a small index and reads forward. Lesson 3 of this track opens those files.

The weak spot is a consumer that falls far behind. It reads old data that is no longer in the page cache, so those reads go to disk and can push recent pages out of memory. One lagging batch job can slow down every reader of the tail on the same broker.

The .index and .timeindex files look huge because Kafka preallocates 10 MiB for the active segment's indexes.

analogy: A partition is a bank's ledger book written in pen. Every line has a number, and new lines go at the bottom. Nobody erases a line: a correction is a new line. Each team that reads the book keeps its own bookmark, and moving your bookmark changes nothing for anyone else. Now and then the archive tears out the oldest pages, whole pages at a time, whether or not anyone has read them. The analogy breaks at scale: a topic is many such books written at the same time, each with its own line numbers, and nothing orders a line in one book against a line in another.
world: Your Quarkus payment services already run on this model. The payments topic is the ledger of record, and settlement, fraud check and notifications are separate consumer groups with separate committed offsets, so a slow notification service never holds up settlement. When a fee bug ships and you must recompute a day of settlements, nobody has to re-send anything. You stop the settlement group and move its offsets back with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets, or you run a one-off job that assigns the partitions and seeks. A Temporal workflow started by a payment event can store that event's topic, partition and offset, which gives an incident review an exact pointer back into the history.
mistake: Treating a topic as a queue that empties itself. A team publishes full card numbers to a topic because "the tokenizer consumes them and then they're gone". Nothing removes them. They stay in the log for the full retention.ms (7 days by default), on every replica, readable by any client allowed to read the topic, and they come back in every replay. People make this mistake because the client API looks like a queue: poll, process, commit. The fix is to choose retention on purpose for every topic and to keep data you may not store for days out of Kafka: tokenize before you produce, or encrypt the field.

compare.title: Read ten records from offset 50 in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: static List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> readTen(KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer) { TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); consumer.seek(tp, 50); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> out = new ArrayList<>(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + Duration.ofSeconds(5).toNanos(); while (out.size() < 10 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).records(tp)) { if (out.size() < 10) out.add(r); } } return out; }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun readTen(consumer: KafkaConsumer<String, String>): List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> { val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) consumer.seek(tp, 50) val out = mutableListOf<ConsumerRecord<String, String>>() val deadline = System.nanoTime() + Duration.ofSeconds(5).toNanos() while (out.size < 10 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) { out += consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).records(tp).take(10 - out.size) } return out }

compare.note: Both call the same Java client library. Kotlin uses listOf where Java uses List.of, adds a whole list with +=, and uses take to stop at ten. records(tp) returns a Java List, so Kotlin's collection functions work on it directly. Neither version commits anything: with assign and no group.id there is no group to commit to.

worked.title: Replay one partition from offset 50 up to where it ended when you started

steps.say: A reconciliation job must re-read partition 0 of payments from offset 50 and stop at the end. But the end moves: producers keep appending while you read. So pin it first, by asking for the end offset before reading anything.
steps.code: // 1. pin the end: the offset the next record would get, right now TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); long stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp);

alt.html: // 1. pin the end: the offset the next record would get, right now val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) val stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp)

steps.say: Set the position. seek only changes a number inside the client; the next poll fetches from there.
steps.code: // 2. set the position consumer.seek(tp, 50);

alt.html: // 2. set the position consumer.seek(tp, 50)

steps.say: Read until the position reaches the pinned end. consumer.position(tp) is the offset of the next record the consumer will return, which makes it the natural stop condition. Records at stopAt or later arrived after you started; leave them for the next run.
steps.code: // 3. read until the position reaches the pinned end while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() >= stopAt) break; // arrived after we started reconcile(r); } }

alt.html: // 3. read until the position reaches the pinned end while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (r in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() >= stopAt) break // arrived after we started reconcile(r) } }

steps.say: Notice what is missing: no group.id and no commit. If the job crashes, you run it again from 50. For a one-off replay that is the simplest correct design. A job that must resume where it stopped needs a group and commits, which is lesson 7 of this track.

lab.title: Build a log in memory, then read a real one
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 12 fail: the stubs throw NotImplementedError or UnsupportedOperationException. The first run also pulls the apache/kafka-native:4.4.0 image (about 150 MB) for the broker tests; after that the broker starts in a second or two.
In MiniLog.kt, write endOffset, append and read. Offsets are dense and start at 0, so the next offset is the number of records so far. read returns a copy and rejects a from outside 0..endOffset.
Write LogReader.poll and LogReader.seek. A reader's whole state is position: read from it, then move it forward by the number of records you got.
Run the tests. The eight tests in MiniLogTest should pass now.
In OffsetReader.java, write readFrom: assign, seek, then a poll loop with a deadline that keeps at most max records.
Run the tests until all 12 pass. OffsetReaderTest runs your code against a real Kafka 4.4 broker in a container.
hints: records.subList(a, b) is a view of the list. Wrap it with .toList() so a caller never sees later appends through it.

In readFrom, consumer.poll(...).records(tp) gives you only that partition's records. The loop needs two exits: enough records, or the deadline passed. Without the deadline, a read at the end of the partition never returns.
If only the broker tests fail with a Docker error, check that Docker Desktop is running. MiniLogTest needs no Docker.

drill.title: Write the replay loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write replay(consumer, topic, partition, from): it reads one partition from offset from up to the end offset as it was when the function started, and returns the values in order. No group, no commits. Then compare with the answer. Did you pin the end offset before the loop?

answer.html: static List<String> replay(Consumer<String, String> consumer, String topic, int partition, long from) { TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(topic, partition); consumer.assign(List.of(tp)); long stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp); // pin the end first consumer.seek(tp, from); List<String> values = new ArrayList<>(); while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp)) { if (r.offset() < stopAt) values.add(r.value()); } } return values; }

alt.html: fun replay(consumer: Consumer<String, String>, topic: String, partition: Int, from: Long): List<String> { val tp = TopicPartition(topic, partition) consumer.assign(listOf(tp)) val stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp) // pin the end first consumer.seek(tp, from) val values = mutableListOf<String>() while (consumer.position(tp) < stopAt) { consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).records(tp) .filter { it.offset() < stopAt } .mapTo(values) { it.value() } } return values }

recap: A queue deletes a message once it is acked; a log keeps every record. A partition is a log: an ordered list of records that only grows at the end, and the broker gives each record the next offset, starting at 0.
An offset never changes and is never reused within a partition, so it names one record for good.
A reader's state is one number per partition: the offset of the next record. A group saves it in __consumer_offsets as its committed offset.
Reading never deletes. Retention removes old data by time or size, whoever has read it.
assign plus seek reads from any offset without a group, so replay costs nothing.
Appends and tail reads are sequential and mostly served from the page cache, which is why the log is fast.

explain.prompt: A colleague who has run IBM MQ and RabbitMQ queues for years asks: "When my consumer acknowledges a Kafka message, where does the message go?" Explain what really happens, and what decides when the record is deleted.
explain.answer: It goes nowhere. Acknowledging in Kafka means committing an offset: the consumer group saves one number per partition, the offset of the next record it will read. The record stays in the partition's log at the same offset, and every other group can still read it, now or later. Kafka deletes old records only through retention, by time (7 days by default) or by size, a whole segment file at a time. So a commit changes only where your group resumes after a restart, and a replay is just moving that number back.

deeper.html:
Jay Kreps' 2013 essay "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction" is worth an evening. (It was published on the LinkedIn engineering blog. The original page has moved, so search for the title.) Its core argument: a log is the simplest structure that gives you a total order of events, and any deterministic process that reads the same log from the same starting point ends up in the same state. Databases already work this way inside. Replication is mostly shipping the log to another machine.

Two ideas from that line of thinking come back later in the course. A table is a log folded down to the latest value per key: Kafka Streams calls this the stream-table duality (the Stream processing track's Kafka Streams lesson), and log compaction (lesson 3 of this track) keeps exactly that latest value per key on disk. And change data capture turns a database's own log into Kafka records (the Stream processing track's lessons on change data capture): Debezium reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, or the Oracle redo log through LogMiner, and publishes each change in commit order.

One detail to keep straight: an offset is a logical number, not a byte position. Records vary in size, so the broker can't compute where offset 50 starts in the file. Each segment file has a sparse index from offsets to byte positions, and lesson 3 of this track opens it.
